questionText: What is abstraction in OOP?
option1: Allowing a class to extend only one parent class
option2: Combining data and methods into a single unit
option3: Hiding complex implementation details and exposing only the essential features/behavior through a defined contract
option4: Restricting direct access to class fields using private
correctOptionExplanation: Abstraction focuses on exposing what an object does via a simple interface, while hiding how it does it internally.

questionText: How is abstraction commonly achieved in Java?
option1: Using only private fields
option2: Using abstract classes and interfaces
option3: Using only static methods
option4: Using only final classes
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes and interfaces are the two primary mechanisms Java provides to define contracts without exposing implementation.

questionText: What is the key difference between abstraction and encapsulation?
option1: They are identical concepts with different names
option2: Abstraction hides implementation complexity behind a contract; encapsulation hides internal data using access modifiers
option3: Abstraction is only for interfaces; encapsulation is only for abstract classes
option4: Encapsulation hides behavior; abstraction hides data
correctOptionExplanation: Abstraction is about design-level hiding of 'how' something works, while encapsulation is about restricting direct access to an object's internal state.

questionText: In `public interface IDiscount { double getDiscount(); }`, what does the method lack?
option1: A return type
option2: A method body/implementation
option3: Parameters
option4: A name
correctOptionExplanation: IDiscount declares getDiscount() without any implementation, only the contract — a core abstraction technique.

questionText: Can IDiscount be instantiated directly with `new IDiscount()`?
option1: Yes, always
option2: Only if it has no methods
option3: Yes, but only inside main()
option4: No, interfaces cannot be instantiated directly
correctOptionExplanation: Interfaces represent contracts, not concrete objects, so they cannot be instantiated without a concrete implementing class.

questionText: In `IDiscount ds = new MembershipDiscount();`, what concept does declaring the variable as IDiscount demonstrate?
option1: Constructor overloading
option2: Abstraction — the calling code depends only on the IDiscount contract, not the concrete class details
option3: Encapsulation of the MembershipDiscount fields
option4: Multiple inheritance of implementation
correctOptionExplanation: Coding against the interface type hides which concrete discount implementation is actually being used from the rest of the program.

questionText: What must MembershipDiscount do to compile successfully as a non-abstract class implementing IDiscount?
option1: Mark the class as final
option2: Declare getDiscount() as private
option3: Provide a concrete implementation of getDiscount()
option4: Leave getDiscount() unimplemented
correctOptionExplanation: Any concrete class implementing an interface must implement all of its abstract methods, or itself be declared abstract.

questionText: Before Java 8, how were interface methods implicitly declared?
option1: protected and static
option2: public and abstract
option3: private and final
option4: package-private and default
correctOptionExplanation: Prior to Java 8's default/static methods, every interface method was implicitly public and abstract.

questionText: Before Java 8, could an interface method have a body?
option1: Yes, but only in abstract classes
option2: Yes, all methods had default bodies
option3: Yes, but only static methods had bodies
option4: No, all methods were implicitly abstract with no body
correctOptionExplanation: Traditional interfaces (pre-Java 8) only declared method signatures; implementation was strictly deferred to implementing classes.

questionText: What are fields declared in an interface implicitly treated as?
option1: private and mutable
option2: transient fields
option3: public, static, and final (constants)
option4: protected instance variables
correctOptionExplanation: Any field declared in an interface is implicitly public static final, meaning it behaves as a constant shared by all implementations.

questionText: Can an interface have instance (non-static) fields holding per-object state?
option1: Yes, but only if marked transient
option2: Yes, freely, just like a class
option3: No, interface fields are always implicitly static (and final), so there is no per-instance state
option4: Yes, but only private ones
correctOptionExplanation: Since interface fields are implicitly static and final, interfaces cannot hold mutable per-instance state — that's left to abstract or concrete classes.

questionText: Can an interface declare a constructor?
option1: No, interfaces cannot have constructors since they can't be instantiated on their own
option2: Yes, but only private constructors
option3: Yes, but only a no-arg constructor
option4: Yes, exactly like a class
correctOptionExplanation: Constructors initialize instance state on object creation, but interfaces have no instantiable state, so constructors aren't allowed.

questionText: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
option1: No, abstract classes can never have constructors
option2: Yes, and it typically runs when a concrete subclass is instantiated via super()
option3: Yes, but it can never be called
option4: Only if the class has no abstract methods
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes can define constructors to initialize shared state, invoked implicitly or explicitly (super()) when a subclass object is created.

questionText: Can an abstract class have instance fields with actual state?
option1: No, all fields become static automatically
option2: No, fields are not allowed in abstract classes
option3: Only public fields are allowed
option4: Yes, unlike traditional interfaces, abstract classes can hold regular instance fields
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes behave like regular classes for fields — they can hold mutable instance state shared by all subclasses.

questionText: What is the correct syntax for declaring an abstract method?
option1: final returnType methodName(parameters);
option2: static returnType methodName(parameters) { }
option3: returnType methodName(parameters) { }
option4: abstract returnType methodName(parameters); with a semicolon and no body
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract methods declare only the signature, ending in a semicolon, with the implementation deferred to a subclass.

questionText: If a class contains even one abstract method, what must be true about the class itself?
option1: The class must be declared final
option2: The class must implement Serializable
option3: The class itself must be declared abstract
option4: The class cannot have a constructor
correctOptionExplanation: Java requires any class containing an abstract method to itself be marked abstract, since it can't be fully instantiated.

questionText: Can an abstract class implement an interface without implementing all of its methods?
option1: Only if the interface has no methods
option2: Yes, as long as the abstract class itself is declared abstract, leaving the remaining methods for concrete subclasses
option3: No, it must implement every method immediately
option4: No, abstract classes cannot implement interfaces at all
correctOptionExplanation: An abstract class may partially implement an interface's methods and leave the rest abstract, to be completed by its own subclasses.

questionText: What core benefit does abstraction provide to the code that depends on IDiscount?
option1: It makes the client code run faster automatically
option2: It hides the method names from the client code
option3: Decoupling — the client code only needs to know the getDiscount() contract, not how each discount type calculates its value
option4: It removes the need for any implementing classes
correctOptionExplanation: Abstraction decouples 'what' a component does from 'how' it does it, so client code depending on IDiscount doesn't care about MembershipDiscount's internal logic.

questionText: If a new CouponDiscount class is added implementing IDiscount, does existing code using IDiscount references need to change?
option1: No, but all subclasses must be recompiled manually every time
option2: Yes, the interface must be redeclared
option3: Yes, every existing usage must be rewritten
option4: No, existing code that depends only on the IDiscount contract continues to work unchanged
correctOptionExplanation: This is the Open/Closed benefit of abstraction: new implementations can be added without modifying code that only depends on the abstract contract.

questionText: What do MembershipDiscount, CreditCardDiscount, and CouponDiscount all implementing IDiscount demonstrate together?
option1: Static binding of methods
option2: Multiple inheritance of class implementation
option3: Abstraction combined with polymorphism — multiple interchangeable implementations behind one shared contract
option4: Encapsulation of private constructors
correctOptionExplanation: This is a classic abstraction + polymorphism pattern: several concrete classes fulfill one abstract contract and can be swapped interchangeably.

questionText: What is exposed to code that only interacts with the IDiscount type?
option1: Only the private fields of MembershipDiscount
option2: Just the method signature/contract (getDiscount()), not the internal calculation logic of the concrete class
option3: Nothing at all; IDiscount is unusable
option4: The full source code of every implementing class
correctOptionExplanation: Abstraction ensures only the essential contract is visible externally; internal calculation details stay encapsulated within each implementation.

questionText: Can a single class implement multiple interfaces (multiple abstraction contracts) in Java?
option1: Yes, a class can implement any number of interfaces
option2: No, only abstract classes can do this
option3: Yes, but only two maximum
option4: No, only one interface per class is allowed
correctOptionExplanation: Java allows implementing multiple interfaces, letting one class fulfill several separate abstraction contracts simultaneously.

questionText: What's the difference in 'how much' abstraction an abstract class vs. a traditional interface provides?
option1: An abstract class always offers 100% abstraction; interfaces offer none
option2: An abstract class can offer partial abstraction (mix of implemented and abstract methods); a traditional interface offered full (100%) abstraction
option3: They provide identical abstraction always
option4: Interfaces cannot provide any abstraction at all
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes can mix concrete and abstract methods (partial abstraction), whereas pre-Java 8 interfaces were fully abstract with no method bodies.

questionText: How did Java 8's default methods change interfaces' relationship to full abstraction?
option1: They removed all abstract methods from interfaces
option2: They eliminated interfaces from the language entirely
option3: They allowed interfaces to provide concrete method bodies, meaning interfaces are no longer necessarily 100% abstract
option4: They made all interface methods private
correctOptionExplanation: Default methods let interfaces supply a working implementation that implementing classes can inherit or override, blurring the old 100%-abstraction rule.

questionText: When should you generally prefer an interface over an abstract class for a contract?
option1: When you want to prevent any other class from ever implementing it
option2: When you need shared constructor logic across a family of related classes
option3: When unrelated classes need to share a capability/contract without a common base implementation or state
option4: When performance is the only concern
correctOptionExplanation: Interfaces suit unrelated classes that just need to agree on a contract, while abstract classes suit closely related classes sharing common code/state.

questionText: When should you generally prefer an abstract class over an interface?
option1: When the type should never have any concrete subclasses
option2: When you want fields to be public static final only
option3: When related subclasses should share common state and partially implemented behavior via inheritance
option4: When you need a class to implement multiple unrelated contracts
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes are appropriate when subclasses are naturally related and benefit from shared fields/constructors/partial implementations.

questionText: What is a real-world analogy for abstraction, like a car's dashboard and steering wheel?
option1: There is no valid real-world analogy for abstraction
option2: The driver interacts with simple controls without needing to understand the engine's internal combustion process
option3: The dashboard exposes every internal engine detail to the driver
option4: The steering wheel is an example of encapsulation, not abstraction
correctOptionExplanation: The driver only needs the 'contract' (steering, pedals) to operate the car; the complex mechanics are hidden — a textbook abstraction analogy.

questionText: What is typically the purpose of a constructor in an abstract class?
option1: To prevent subclassing entirely
option2: To override methods from java.lang.Object only
option3: To initialize shared fields/state that all concrete subclasses will inherit when instantiated
option4: To allow the abstract class itself to be instantiated directly
correctOptionExplanation: Even though the abstract class itself can't be instantiated, its constructor runs (via super()) to set up common state whenever a subclass object is created.

questionText: Can you write `IDiscount x = new IDiscount();` directly?
option1: No, this is invalid — you must instantiate a concrete class that implements IDiscount
option2: Yes, but only inside a static method
option3: Yes, this is always valid Java
option4: Yes, but only if IDiscount has fields
correctOptionExplanation: Interfaces cannot be instantiated directly; you must create an object of a class that implements the interface, then assign it to an interface-typed variable.

questionText: Is `IDiscount` still usable as a variable/parameter/return type even though it can't be instantiated directly?
option1: Only inside the same package as its implementations
option2: Only as a return type, never as a parameter type
option3: No, interfaces cannot be used as types anywhere in code
option4: Yes, interfaces are valid types for variables, parameters, and return values, referencing any implementing object
correctOptionExplanation: Interfaces function as full types in Java's type system — they just can't be instantiated without pointing to a concrete implementing object.

questionText: What happens if MembershipDiscount fails to implement the getDiscount() method from IDiscount?
option1: A compile-time error occurs, since a concrete class must implement all abstract methods of the interfaces it implements
option2: The method silently returns 0.0 at runtime
option3: Java automatically generates a default implementation
option4: The program compiles but throws a runtime exception
correctOptionExplanation: Java enforces at compile time that a concrete class implementing an interface provides bodies for all its abstract methods.

questionText: Can one interface extend another interface?
option1: Only using the implements keyword
option2: No, interfaces cannot extend other interfaces
option3: Only if both interfaces are empty
option4: Yes, using the extends keyword, inheriting its abstract method declarations
correctOptionExplanation: Interfaces can extend other interfaces (even multiple ones) using extends, forming interface inheritance hierarchies.

questionText: Can an interface extend multiple other interfaces at once?
option1: Yes, unlike classes, an interface can extend multiple interfaces simultaneously
option2: Only abstract classes can do this
option3: No, interfaces cannot extend anything
option4: No, an interface can only extend one other interface
correctOptionExplanation: Java allows multiple interface inheritance for interfaces themselves, since there's no shared implementation state to create ambiguity.

questionText: What is a 'marker interface' (like the classic Serializable)?
option1: An abstract class with no fields
option2: An interface that must have at least 10 methods
option3: A private interface accessible only within one class
option4: An interface with no methods at all, used purely to tag/mark a class with some meta-property
correctOptionExplanation: Marker interfaces contain no abstract methods; they exist purely to signal a capability or property to the runtime or framework via type-checking.

questionText: Can an abstract class be declared as final?
option1: No, marking an abstract class final would make it both unextendable and uninstantiable, so it's contradictory and disallowed
option2: Yes, this is a common and valid pattern
option3: Yes, but only in interfaces
option4: Yes, but only if it has no abstract methods
correctOptionExplanation: final prevents subclassing, but an abstract class must be subclassed to ever be used, so declaring it final and abstract together is invalid.

questionText: Since Java 9, can interfaces have private methods?
option1: No, interfaces can never declare private methods
option2: Yes, private methods let default/static methods share internal helper logic without exposing it publicly
option3: Yes, but only public methods are actually allowed
option4: No, private methods are only allowed in enums
correctOptionExplanation: Java 9 introduced private interface methods so default/static methods could share reusable logic internally without polluting the public API.

questionText: What is a key trait of static methods declared in an interface?
option1: They must be overridden by every implementing class
option2: They belong to the interface itself, are not inherited by implementing classes, and cannot be overridden
option3: They automatically become abstract in subclasses
option4: They can only be called via an instance of an implementing class
correctOptionExplanation: Interface static methods are invoked on the interface type directly (e.g., IDiscount.someUtility()) and aren't part of the polymorphic contract implementing classes inherit.

questionText: Does abstraction reduce complexity specifically for the code that consumes an abstraction?
option1: It has no effect on complexity at all
option2: No, it always increases the complexity for consuming code
option3: Yes, consuming code only needs to understand the simple contract, not the full implementation details
option4: It only affects the implementing class's internal complexity
correctOptionExplanation: The whole point of abstraction is to let consuming code work with a minimal, well-defined contract instead of needing to understand every implementation detail.

questionText: Which keyword is used to declare an interface in Java?
option1: abstract
option2: implements
option3: class
option4: interface
correctOptionExplanation: The interface keyword defines a new interface type in Java.

questionText: Which keyword marks a class or method as abstract?
option1: final
option2: abstract
option3: interface
option4: static
correctOptionExplanation: The abstract keyword is used both for abstract classes and for abstract methods lacking an implementation.

questionText: Can an abstract class contain a main() method used to test its concrete subclasses?
option1: Yes, an abstract class can have a main method just like any other class
option2: No, abstract classes can never define a main method
option3: Only if the class has zero abstract methods
option4: Only interfaces can have a main method
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes support any valid class member, including a main method, even though the abstract class itself can't be instantiated.

questionText: Is abstraction primarily a runtime mechanism or a design-time concept?
option1: It's identical to garbage collection
option2: It's purely a runtime performance optimization
option3: It only exists at the bytecode level
option4: It's primarily a design-time concept about hiding implementation complexity behind a clean contract
correctOptionExplanation: Abstraction is a design principle for structuring code around contracts, distinct from runtime mechanisms like binding or garbage collection.

questionText: Does using abstraction generally require an inheritance-like relationship (extends/implements)?
option1: Yes, a class must extend an abstract class or implement an interface to fulfill its contract
option2: No, abstraction requires no relationship between classes at all
option3: Abstraction requires generics exclusively
option4: Only composition can establish abstraction, never inheritance
correctOptionExplanation: To actually provide the behavior behind an abstract contract, a class must extend the abstract class or implement the interface defining that contract.

questionText: How does abstraction differ from encapsulation using the discount example?
option1: IDiscount hides which calculation strategy is used (abstraction); each discount class hiding its own internal fields is encapsulation
option2: There is no meaningful difference between them
option3: They are the exact same technique applied to the same fields
option4: Abstraction hides fields; encapsulation hides methods
correctOptionExplanation: Abstraction here is about hiding which concrete discount strategy runs behind the IDiscount contract; encapsulation is each class protecting its own internal data with private fields and access modifiers.

questionText: What is a 'functional interface' and how does it relate to abstraction?
option1: An interface that cannot be used with generics
option2: A class implementing zero interfaces
option3: An interface with exactly one abstract method, representing the minimal possible abstraction usable with a lambda expression
option4: Any interface with static methods only
correctOptionExplanation: Functional interfaces reduce an abstraction down to a single abstract method, which is precisely what a lambda expression can satisfy.

questionText: If IDiscount had exactly one abstract method, could `IDiscount d = () -> 10.0;` work as valid abstraction usage?
option1: No, lambdas cannot implement interfaces
option2: Yes, IDiscount would qualify as a functional interface, and the lambda becomes its concrete implementation at that call site
option3: No, interfaces with fields can never be functional interfaces
option4: Only static classes can be assigned this way
correctOptionExplanation: A single-abstract-method interface can be satisfied inline by a lambda expression, which is treated as an anonymous implementation fulfilling the abstraction.

questionText: Why is abstraction considered important for testability?
option1: It prevents mocking frameworks from working
option2: Client code can depend on an interface and swap in a fake/mock implementation during tests instead of the real one
option3: It removes the need to write tests entirely
option4: It forces all tests to use static methods
correctOptionExplanation: Because code depends on the abstract contract rather than a concrete class, tests can substitute lightweight mock implementations that satisfy the same interface.

questionText: What would be the effect of removing the IDiscount interface and instead hardcoding MembershipDiscount everywhere it's used?
option1: It would make the code more abstract, not less
option2: It would tightly couple the code to one specific discount type, making it harder to add or swap discount strategies later
option3: It would have no effect on flexibility or maintainability
option4: It would automatically improve performance with no downsides
correctOptionExplanation: Removing the shared abstraction and hardcoding a concrete class increases coupling, directly undermining the flexibility abstraction was providing.

questionText: Can an abstract class extend another abstract class without implementing its abstract methods?
option1: Yes, an abstract class can extend another abstract class and leave abstract methods unimplemented for further subclasses
option2: No, this is always a compile-time error
option3: No, only interfaces can extend other interfaces
option4: Yes, but only if it has zero methods of its own
correctOptionExplanation: Since an abstract class isn't required to be instantiable, it can extend another abstract class and defer implementing inherited abstract methods to its own subclasses.

questionText: Overall, what is the main design payoff of using abstraction well?
option1: Improved maintainability and extensibility, since implementation details can change or grow without breaking dependent code
option2: Complete elimination of the need for interfaces or abstract classes
option3: Guaranteed faster runtime performance in every case
option4: Automatic thread-safety for all classes
correctOptionExplanation: Good abstraction isolates change: as long as the contract stays stable, implementations can evolve or multiply without breaking the rest of the system.
